title: Computational reconstruction of organism-scale molecular maps

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a general computational system that turns molecular measurements from a whole biological specimen into a validated three-dimensional map of its cells and molecular states. It would place cell boundaries, RNA and protein measurements, and spatial relationships into a common coordinate system, while reporting where information is missing and how uncertain each reconstruction is. The intended capability extends from intact small organisms to large mammalian tissue volumes; achieving one would not automatically establish the other.

The central computational work comprises inferring spatial positions, aligning measurements from different modalities, assigning molecular signals to cells, and validating the resulting map. Existing studies illustrate complementary foundations: volumetric DNA microscopy infers molecular coordinates from molecular relationships, including through geodesic spectral embeddings, while DBiTplus registers sequencing-based transcriptomics with multiplexed protein imaging on the same tissue section. Extending these foundations into a general system would also require suitable specimen preparation and molecular measurement methods.

significance.text: If validated and made routinely usable, this capability would provide a shared spatial representation of molecular anatomy across entire specimens. Researchers could examine how molecular states relate to cell neighborhoods and tissue organization, and compare specimens or developmental stages without assembling every modality into a separate, partly disconnected account. The revolutionary advance would be the combination of breadth, reliable cellular assignment, three-dimensional coverage and practical accessibility, rather than spatial mapping alone, which the supplied studies already demonstrate in bounded forms.

As a conditional downstream possibility, sufficiently comparable maps could support more systematic studies of developmental variation, disease-associated tissue changes and interactions among cell populations. Their usefulness would depend on molecular coverage, reconstruction accuracy and consistency across specimens. A common coordinate system would make these comparisons possible; it would not by itself establish predictive biological models or explain the mechanisms producing an observed pattern.

Making organization inspectable through a validated map is different from observing every molecule directly. Spatial inference and transcriptomic deconvolution remain model-dependent, and an apparently detailed map can contain inferred assignments and measurement gaps. Spatial association does not establish causation. Similarly, comparing fixed specimens or arranging cell states along an inferred trajectory does not track the same living organism over time: the supplied DNA microscopy demonstration used fixed, permeabilized embryos. Causal and longitudinal claims would require additional experiments.

missing_breakthrough.text: The proposed missing capability is scalable, accurate integration of molecular identity, cell boundaries and spatial relationships across whole specimens, with explicit accounting for uncertainty and missing measurements. The supplied studies identify important obstacles to this endpoint, but they do not establish the field-wide absence of such a system at a later date. The breakthrough would require reconstruction that remains reliable as specimen size, tissue complexity and the number of measured molecular features increase.

A major barrier is obtaining enough spatially informative molecular measurements throughout the specimen. Volumetric DNA microscopy identifies computational scalability challenges and spatial gaps, and states that organism-wide single-cell resolution requires further chemistry optimization. Its discussion also identifies improved sequence capture and prospective proteomic acquisition as development needs. DBiTplus documents coverage–resolution trade-offs and warns that low capture depth can cause low-abundance transcripts to drop out. Reconstruction therefore depends on improvements in measurement as well as computation; absent signals cannot simply be treated as confirmed biological absence.

Integration presents a separate challenge. A system must align modalities, identify cell boundaries and distinguish measured molecular signals from signals allocated through a model. DBiTplus uses imaging-guided, reference-informed deconvolution to divide transcriptomic spots into cell-type sub-spots. That supports useful integration, but it does not turn every inferred expression assignment into a direct transcript measurement from an individual cell. General reconstruction would need to preserve this distinction while addressing incomplete biological annotation and the additional alignment problems involved in extending section-based measurements through a volume.

A proposed engineering requirement is to propagate uncertainty through spatial inference, registration and cell assignment, rather than attaching confidence only to the final visualization. The system should distinguish unmeasured regions, molecular dropout, ambiguous cell assignments and genuinely low or absent expression. These are requirements for a convincing general system, not source-defined completion standards or capabilities already established by the supplied demonstrations.

current_state.text: Qian and Weinstein’s volumetric DNA microscopy study, published online on 27 March 2025, reconstructed transcriptomic spatial organization in intact zebrafish embryos. It inferred coordinates computationally and demonstrated whole-embryo spatial organization, but explicitly did not achieve single-cell resolution throughout the organism. The reviewed text also reports agreement of spatial expression with Stereo-seq. These results establish a foundation for organism-scale spatial inference; they do not demonstrate comprehensive RNA–protein mapping with individually resolved cells everywhere.

Enninful and colleagues’ DBiTplus study, published online on 15 January 2026, combined spatial transcriptomics and multiplexed protein imaging on the same tissue section. Its computational framework registers imaging-derived cell information with transcriptomic spots and produces an integrated representation containing molecular features, cell-type labels and spatial coordinates. Transcriptomic spot splitting uses imaging guidance and reference-informed deconvolution, so inferred cell-type expression must be distinguished from direct transcript measurements in individual cells. Same-section integration is an important demonstrated capability, but it does not establish intact-organism, three-dimensional multimodal reconstruction.

Neither supplied study establishes routine, comprehensive, organism-scale multimodal reconstruction. Organism-wide single-cell resolution, improved sequence capture and proteomic extension are development needs or prospective directions in the reviewed DNA microscopy discussion, rather than completed achievements. The proposed extension to large mammalian volumes likewise remains beyond what these two demonstrations establish.

Interpretation is limited by the supplied review’s document coverage. The DNA microscopy extraction includes substantial main text and methods, but pages 18–20 have no extracted text and figures were not inspected. For DBiTplus, both retained HTML and a main-article PDF contain identifiable, inspectable article text; the earlier statement that its PDF fetch failed does not accurately describe the retained evidence. However, both copies are truncated, and the PDF has missing-text and form-content extraction warnings. These limitations constrain completeness of assessment without showing that the reported results are false. This record relies on the supplied review and does not claim a new inspection of those documents.

The supplied freshness record is empty. Consequently, the dated studies support the bounded achievements described here, but do not establish whether the broader capability remained unresolved across the field as of 1 November 2026. Later retrieval timestamps establish when copies were saved, not that subsequent developments were comprehensively searched.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: produce independently validated three-dimensional reconstructions for multiple intact small organisms and large mammalian tissue volumes, resolving individual cells and integrating broad RNA and protein measurements within one spatial framework. The demonstration should report which regions and molecular features were measured, which assignments were inferred and where coverage is incomplete. These are proposed criteria for this innovation, not established consensus standards.
completion_criteria.label: Validated cellular maps span small organisms and large mammalian volumes

completion_criteria.text: Proposed validation should compare reconstructed positions, cell boundaries and molecular-to-cell assignments against independent measurements. It should test whether reported uncertainty predicts observed errors and whether missingness estimates distinguish measurement failure from biological absence. Direct measurements and deconvolved expression should be evaluated separately, so a model’s agreement with its own reference assumptions is not mistaken for independent confirmation.
completion_criteria.label: Independent measurements validate reconstructions, uncertainty calibration and missingness estimates

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical tests should include independent laboratories, repeated specimens and a deliberately varied set of tissues and organism types. Before evaluation, the benchmark would need explicit choices for organism diversity, mammalian tissue volume, RNA and protein coverage, acceptable localization and assignment errors, uncertainty calibration, missingness definitions, computational requirements, cost and preparation time. Routine usability would require outside laboratories to reproduce useful maps within those declared bounds. Success across a finite test set would establish demonstrated breadth, not literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Outside laboratories reproduce useful maps within declared benchmark bounds

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: BIF-01, “A predictive decoder for the regulatory genome,” and BIF-06, “A general decoder for unknown gene and protein functions,” concern interpreting biological sequence or molecular function. BIF-07 would supply spatial context in which regulatory activity and molecular functions could be studied. Locating expression does not itself decode regulatory rules or establish an unknown molecule’s function.

Roster-based synthesis: BIF-02, “Predictive molecular dynamics from biological sequence,” and BIF-09, “Proteome-scale prediction of molecular interactions and affinities,” address molecular behavior and binding. Organism-scale maps could constrain where molecules coexist and where interactions are plausible. Spatial proximity alone does not determine binding affinity, molecular dynamics or whether an interaction actually occurs.

Roster-based synthesis: BIF-03, “A transferable, predictive virtual cell,” BIF-04, “General reconstruction of causal cellular networks,” and BIF-08, “Reliable reconstruction and forecasting of single-cell fates,” overlap through their need for well-characterized cellular states and context. BIF-07 could provide spatial observations for building or testing those systems. A spatial map remains distinct from a predictive cell simulator, an identified causal network or a validated forecast of a cell’s future fate.

Roster-based synthesis: BIF-05, “Computer-aided design of functional whole genomes,” and BIF-13, “Predictive design of functional genetic circuits and pathways,” concern designing biological systems. Molecular maps could help characterize the spatial consequences of a design or reveal tissue-specific constraints. Reconstructing an existing specimen does not establish the ability to design a genome, circuit or pathway that will function as intended.

Roster-based synthesis: BIF-11, “Accessible, uncertainty-aware assembly of complex genomes,” shares reconstruction and uncertainty-management concerns, but its target is genome sequence organization rather than three-dimensional cellular anatomy. BIF-12, “Strain-resolved discovery and functional profiling of microbial communities,” could overlap where spatial maps describe community organization, while retaining a separate focus on strain identity and functional profiling. BIF-10, “A broadly capable autonomous bioinformatics discovery system,” might use spatial reconstruction as one component of a wider discovery workflow; BIF-07 does not itself require or establish autonomous discovery.

unresolved_issues: The empty freshness record leaves field-wide progress through 1 November 2026 unverified.

Operational benchmark choices remain unspecified: organism diversity, mammalian volume, molecular coverage, acceptable errors, uncertainty calibration, missingness definitions, computational resources, cost and preparation limits.

The supplied evidence does not establish that measurement and reconstruction methods can jointly deliver broad RNA–protein coverage with reliable individual-cell assignment throughout intact organisms and large mammalian volumes.
Incomplete extraction, truncated DBiTplus copies and uninspected DNA microscopy figures limit the completeness of the supplied assessment.
An earlier DBiTplus PDF-fetch failure may have occurred, but no evidence supplied here verifies that separate event; the retained main-article PDF supports correcting the record.

brief.title: Whole specimens mapped cell by cell
possible: Researchers could explore a whole small organism or a large volume of mammalian tissue as a three-dimensional map. They could see cell boundaries, RNA—molecules that reflect gene activity—and proteins in their shared locations, with gaps and uncertain assignments marked.
why: A shared map would help researchers connect molecular activity with neighboring cells and tissue structure. They could compare specimens and stages of development without piecing together separate maps for each kind of measurement.
Comparable maps could support systematic studies of developmental differences, disease-related tissue changes and interactions among cell populations.

sources.who: Nianchao Qian and Joshua A. Weinstein
sources.showed: They inferred molecular positions throughout intact zebrafish embryos from interactions between molecular tags. The reconstructed shapes and gene activity patterns matched known anatomy.
sources.quote:
Applying whole-transcriptome 
volumetric DNA microscopy to intact zebrafish embryos, we demonstrate 
that three-dimensional image inference recapitulates zebrafish 
morphology and known gene expression patterns, capturing the spatial 
organization of gene sequences.
sources.cited_for: Molecular relationships can support spatial reconstruction across an intact small organism.
sources.not_established: The work did not resolve individual cells throughout the organism or combine broad RNA and protein measurements.

sources.showed: Their DBiTplus method combined RNA measurements and protein images from the same tissue slice. Software aligned the measurements and estimated gene activity for different cell types.
sources.quote:
We demonstrate DBiTplus across diverse samples 
including frozen mouse embryos, and formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded 
human lymph nodes and lymphoma tissues, highlighting its compatibility 
with challenging clinical specimens.
sources.cited_for: RNA measurements and protein imaging can be integrated on the same tissue slice.
sources.not_established: The work did not reconstruct a whole organism in three dimensions; some cell-level RNA assignments were model estimates.

shown: Qian and Weinstein reconstructed molecular organization across intact zebrafish embryos, without resolving every cell. Enninful and colleagues combined RNA measurements and protein imaging on tissue slices, using models to estimate how shared RNA signals divide among cell types.
missing: Validated maps still need to combine broad RNA and protein measurements with individual cell boundaries throughout whole specimens.
Measurements need enough coverage to distinguish molecules missed by the method from molecules that are truly absent.
Reconstructions need to carry uncertainty through position estimates, alignment and cell assignment, while distinguishing measurements from model estimates.
Outside laboratories still need to reproduce useful maps across varied specimens within stated limits on accuracy, cost and preparation time.

milestones.label: Validated cellular maps across organisms and large mammalian tissue volumes
milestones.explanation: Independently validated maps would have to resolve cells and broad RNA and protein coverage across multiple intact small organisms and large mammalian tissue volumes. This would establish breadth while marking inferred assignments and gaps.

milestones.label: Independent checks confirm accuracy, uncertainty and measurement gaps
milestones.explanation: Independent measurements would have to check positions, boundaries, cell assignments, error estimates and measurement gaps, assessing model estimates separately. This would establish whether the maps and their confidence reports are trustworthy.

milestones.label: Outside laboratories reproduce useful maps within agreed limits
milestones.explanation: Outside laboratories would have to reproduce maps across repeated, varied specimens within declared limits on coverage, error, computing, cost and preparation. This would establish practical usability across the tested range.

uncertain: It remains unclear whether measurement and computation can jointly deliver broad RNA and protein coverage with reliable cell assignment at both scales.
The required specimen diversity, tissue volume, molecular coverage and acceptable errors, costs and preparation times remain to be defined.
Spatial patterns alone cannot establish causes, and comparisons of fixed specimens cannot track the same living organism over time.

page.title: Whole-specimen 3D spatial multi-omics reconstruction
page.definition: A computational reconstruction places cell boundaries, RNA measurements and protein measurements in a shared three-dimensional coordinate system throughout a specimen. RNA measurements describe gene expression. Whole specimens comprise intact small organisms or complete mammalian organs.

goal.need: A zebrafish embryo 24 hours after fertilization contains about 25,000 cells. At 10 million molecular tags, the mean is 400 tags per cell. Connecting these measurements to cellular neighborhoods requires spatial assignment throughout the specimen. DBiTplus demonstrates why integration matters by aligning transcriptome-wide RNA sampling with cell-resolved protein imaging on the same section.

completion.title: Whole-organism and whole-organ 3D RNA–protein cell maps are reproduced across laboratories.
completion.criterion: The same reconstruction workflow produces a cellular 3D RNA–protein map of a complete specimen in each class. Whole-transcriptome RNA measurements, multiplexed protein measurements and cell boundaries share coordinates. Independent spatial measurements validate localization and cellular assignments, and independent laboratories reproduce cell profiles and tissue organization in replicate specimens. Measured, inferred and unmeasured features are identifiable.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas, qualitative synthesis of the cited mapping and validation goals.
completion.basis: Searches of HuBMAP funding calls and assay definitions, the HCA white paper, the SpaceTx roadmap, and spatial-omics standards and challenges found no joint whole-specimen completion test. The Atlas combines their spatial, multimodal and reproducibility goals into a qualitative test. Each specimen class requires its own demonstration. The mammalian scope follows HuBMAP's whole-organ target.

milestones.title: An in-situ assay demonstrates molecular mapping inside tissue.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate an in-situ molecular-mapping method with initial experimental validation. Qian and Weinstein reconstructed 3D molecular organization in four fixed zebrafish embryos collected 24 hours after fertilization, recovering morphology and known expression patterns. Their paper was published online on 27 March 2025.
milestones.set_by: NIH HuBMAP, RFA-RM-21-026, description of Transformative Technology Development. The programme's original scope is human tissue mapping.

milestones.title: Detected biomolecules are reproducibly assigned to cells or extracellular compartments.
milestones.criterion: Assign detected biomolecules reliably and reproducibly to individual cells or extracellular compartments. NIH describes a typical length scale around 1 μm, allowing proposals within an order of magnitude according to tissue and analyte. Qian and Weinstein report spatial gaps limiting organism-wide single-cell resolution. DBiTplus estimates cell-type RNA profiles through reference-informed decomposition of multicellular spots.
milestones.set_by: NIH HuBMAP Frequently Asked Questions, question 14, definition of a high-resolution assay. The definition was written for human tissues.
milestones.threshold_quote: reliably and reproducibly assign detected biomolecules to individual cells or extracellular compartments of a tissue.

milestones.title: RNA and protein expression are mapped in three dimensions across a whole organ.
milestones.criterion: Map RNA and protein expression in three dimensions across an entire organ. DBiTplus provides section-level evidence through co-registered RNA measurements and protein images from one benign human lymph-node section at 50-μm RNA sampling resolution with a 35-protein panel. That demonstration was published on 15 January 2026.
milestones.set_by: NIH HuBMAP, RFA-RM-17-025, Research Focus. This whole-organ target was written for human mapping. For an intact organism, an organ map is an intermediate result.
milestones.threshold_quote: multi-parameter mapping of RNA and protein expression in three dimensions across whole organs

milestones.title: A whole-specimen RNA–protein map recovers cell populations in the correct proportions.
milestones.criterion: In a whole-specimen 3D RNA–protein reconstruction, recover cell populations up to a predefined rarity threshold, in the correct proportions and with appropriate molecular profiles. Compare aggregate RNA or protein measurements and intact-tissue spatial measurements with the reconstructed profiles. Molecular populations must correspond to validated biological entities or independently distinguishable histological features. These are HCA's integrity and predictive-value tests.
milestones.set_by: Human Cell Atlas consortium, white paper dated 18 October 2017, validation protocol. The tests were written for human draft atlases and are applied separately to the two specimen classes here.
milestones.threshold_quote: Integrity is defined by the ability to capture all cells in the tissue in the correct proportions and appropriate profiles.

not_found: No common numerical limits were found for specimen volume, molecular coverage, reconstruction error or uncertainty calibration.
